passages.original: 6. Denique in illo libro , ubi illa capitula Pelagius scripsit, huic positioni •, qua dixit, « Omnes voluntate propria regi, et suo desiderio unumquemque dimitti , 1 subjecit aliquid de testimonio Scripturarum , quo satis appareat non se sibi hominem regendum debere committere. Ait enim de boc ipso Sapientia k Salomonis : Sum quidem et ego mortalis homo, similis omnium, ex genere terreno illius qui prior finctus est 5; et caetera usque ad eum capituli finem, ubi legitur, Unus ergo ommbus introitus ad vitam, et simiiis exitus : propter hoc optavi, et datus est mihi sensus, et invocavi, et verrit in me spiritus sapientiœ (Sap. vn, i-7). Nonne luce clarius apparet, quemadmodum iste considerata miseria fragililalis humanæ, non est ausus se regendum sibi committere ; sed optavit, et datus est ei sensus, de quo dicit Apostolus, Nos autem sensum Domini habemus (I Cor. II, 16); et invocavii, et vcnit in eum spiritns sapientiae? Hoc enim spiritu, non viribus propriae voluntatis, reguntur et aguntur qui filii sunt Dei.
passages.english: 6. Finally, in that book where Pelagius wrote those chapters, to this proposition, in which he said, "All are ruled by their own will, and each is left to his own desire," he added something from the testimony of the Scriptures, from which it is quite clear that a man ought not to entrust himself to himself to be ruled. For the Wisdom of Solomon says about this very thing: I too am indeed a mortal man, like all, of the earthly race of him who was first formed; and the rest up to the end of that chapter, where we read, So there is one entrance into life for all, and a like exit: for this reason I prayed, and understanding was given to me, and I called upon [God], and the spirit of wisdom came into me (Wisd. 7:1-7). Is it not clearer than light how this man, having considered the misery of human frailty, did not dare to entrust himself to himself to be ruled; but he prayed, and understanding was given to him, of which the Apostle says, But we have the mind of the Lord (1 Cor. 2:16); and he called upon [God], and the spirit of wisdom came into him? For it is by this spirit, not by the powers of their own will, that those who are sons of God are ruled and led.
passages.notes: The Latin 'sensus' is rendered both 'understanding' (Wisdom) and 'mind' (1 Cor.); Augustine links the two through the same word.

passages.original: 9. Item recitatum est quod in libro suo Pelagius posuit, < In die judicii iniquis ct peccatoribus non esse parcendum, sed æternis eos ignibus exurendos. a Quod ideo fratres moverat, ut objicienduni putaretur, quod ita dictum est, tanquam omnes peccatores a terno essent supplicio puniendi, non eis exceptis qui fundamentum babent Christum , quamvis superirdificent ligna.
passages.english: 9. Likewise there was read out what Pelagius had set down in his book: "On the day of judgement the wicked and sinners are not to be spared, but are to be burned up in eternal fires." This had troubled the brothers, so that they thought it should be raised as an objection, because it was said in such a way as though all sinners were to be punished with eternal punishment, not excepting those who have Christ as their foundation, even though they build wood upon it.

passages.original: Quod autem addidit Pelagius, < Et si quis aliter credit, Origenista est: > hoc acceperunt judices, quod revera in Origene dignissime detestatur Ecclesia, id est, quod etiam illi quos Dominus dicit aeterno supplicio puniendos, et ipse diabolus atque angeli ejus, post tempus licet prelixum purgati liberabuntur a poenis, et sanctis cum Deo regnantibus societate beatitudinis adhærebunt. Hoc ergo Synodus dixit, < alienum non esse ab Ecclesia, > non secundum Pelagium , sed potius secundum Evangelium , quod tales iniqui et peccatores æternis ignibus exurentur, quales tali supplicio dignos judicat Evangelium ; et quod detestabiliter cum Origene sentiat , quisquis dixerit aliquando eorum finiri posse supplicium, quod Dommus dixit aeternum. De illis vero peccatoribus, quos dicit Apostolus , exusto eorum opere, tanquam per ignem salvos futuros , quoniam nihil Pelagio de iis evidenter objectum est , nihil jadicavcrunt. Quapropter, qui dicit iniquos et peccatores, quos æterno supplicio veritas damoat, aliquando inde posse liberari , non inconvenienlor eum Pelagius Origenistam vocat : sed rursus, qui nullum peccatorem in Dei judicio misericordia dignum existimat, quodvultei nomen imponat, dum tamen et hunc errorem ecclesiastica veritate non recipi intelligat.
passages.english: But as for what Pelagius added, "And if anyone believes otherwise, he is an Origenist," the judges took this to mean what the Church most rightly detests in Origen, namely, that even those whom the Lord says are to be punished with eternal punishment, and the devil himself and his angels, will, after a time however long, be purified and freed from their punishments, and will be joined in a fellowship of blessedness with the saints reigning with God. So the Synod said that this was "not foreign to the Church," not according to Pelagius but rather according to the Gospel: that such wicked people and sinners will be burned in eternal fires as the Gospel judges worthy of such punishment; and that whoever says that their punishment, which the Lord called eternal, can at some time be ended, holds a detestable view along with Origen. But concerning those sinners whom the Apostle says will be saved as through fire, once their work has been burned up, they made no judgement, since nothing about them had been clearly objected against Pelagius. Therefore, whoever says that the wicked and sinners whom the truth condemns to eternal punishment can at some time be freed from it, Pelagius not unfittingly calls him an Origenist; but on the other hand, as for one who thinks that no sinner is worthy of mercy in God's judgement, let him give him whatever name he likes, provided he understands that this error too is not accepted by the truth of the Church.

passages.original: CAPUT IV. — 12. Objectum est et iliud Pelagio, tanquam in suo libro scripserit, < Malum nec in cogitationem venire. > Respondit autem, < Hoc non ita posuimus; sed diximus, debere studere Christianum, ne male cagitet: > quod, sicut decuit, episcopiapprobarunt. Quis enim dubitat, malum cogitari non oportere?
passages.english: CHAPTER IV. — 12. This too was objected against Pelagius, as though he had written in his book, "Evil does not even come into thought." But he replied, "We did not set it down so; rather we said that a Christian ought to strive not to think evil": which the bishops, as was fitting, approved. For who doubts that evil ought not to be thought?

Kgo vero Scripturarum auctoritatem secutus dixi, quoniam in propheta Daniele scriptum est, Et accipient sancti regntim Altissimi » (Dan.
passages.english: CHAPTER V. — 13. So when the judges had approved this reply of Pelagius too, another [statement] was read out which he wrote in his little book: "The kingdom of heaven was promised even in the Old Testament." To which Pelagius [said]: "This can also be proved through the Scriptures; but heretics deny it, to the injury of the Old Testament. I, however, following the authority of the Scriptures, said it, since it is written in the prophet Daniel, And the saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High" (Dan.
passages.notes: The citation is completed in the following passage (7:18).

passages.original: xix, 10, 11). Iloc ergo episcopi Ecclesiam recipere pronuntiarunt, quod plus sit virginitas perseverans, quæ præcepta non est, quam nuptiarum castitas, quae præcepta est. Quo autem sensu illud Pelagius , sie Cœlestius dixerit, judices nescierunt.
passages.english: 19:10-11). So the bishops declared that the Church accepts this: that persevering virginity, which is not commanded, is something greater than the chastity of marriage, which is commanded. But in what sense Pelagius or Caelestius said it, the judges did not know.

passages.original: Sod quod ista sequitur, me rursum sollicitat. Cum enim de quinto capitulo libri Cœlestii huic fuisset objectum, quod « affirment unumquemque hom!nem OMnes virtutes posse habere et gr.itas, et auferant diversitatem gratiarum, quam Apostolus docet: i Pelagius respondit, « Dictum est a nobis, sed maligne et imperite reprehenderunt. Non enim auferimus gratiarum diversitatem : scd dicimus donare Dcum ei qui fuerit dignus accipere, omnes gratias, sicut Paulo apostolo donavil.
passages.english: But what follows troubles me again. For when, concerning the fifth chapter of Caelestius' book, it had been objected against him that they "affirm that every man can have all virtues and graces, and take away the diversity of graces which the Apostle teaches," Pelagius replied, "It was said by us, but they have criticized it maliciously and ignorantly. For we do not take away the diversity of graces; but we say that God gives to him who is worthy to receive [them] all graces, as he gave [them] to the apostle Paul.

passages.original: Ipsc clamat, ipsc testatur, ipse ut in se Dei dona commendet, nec in si ipso, sed in Domino glorietur 1 ( I Cor. i, 51), non soli nt nulla ac habuisse dicit mcrila boua, ut apostohis fieret ; scd etiam mata merita sua dicit, ut Dei gratiaminanirestet et prædicet. Non sum, inquit, idoneus vocan apostolus : quod quid est aliud, quam , Non som dignus? nam hoc plerique latini codices liabent. Hoc est nempe quod quicrimus : nempe isto munere apostolatus illæ omnes gratiæ continentur. Non eniin decebat aut oportebat apostolum non habere prophetiam , aut non essc dofHorcm, aut non clarescere virtutibus donationibusque sanitatum, aut adjutoria non præbere, aut Ecclesias non gubernare, auMinguarum generibus non excellere. Omnia hæc unum nomcn apostolatus amplectitur. ipsum igitur consulamus ; ipsum potius audiamus : dicamus ci. Sancte Paule apostole, Pelagius monachus dignum td dicit fuisse, qui acciperes omnes gratias apostolatus tui; tu ipse quid dicis ? Non sum, inquit, dignus vocari apostolus ! itane, ut deferam honorem Paulo. Pelagio magis de Paulo credere audebo, quam Paulo ?
passages.english: He himself cries out, he himself testifies, so that he may commend God's gifts in himself, and glory not in himself but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31); he says not only that he had no good merits by which he might become an apostle, but he even states his evil merits, so as to show forth and proclaim the grace of God. I am not fit, he says, to be called an apostle: and what is this but, I am not worthy? for most Latin manuscripts have this. This is surely what we are asking about: for surely all those graces are contained in this gift of apostleship. For it was not fitting or necessary for an apostle not to have prophecy, or not to be a teacher, or not to be renowned for mighty works and gifts of healing, or not to provide helps, or not to govern churches, or not to excel in kinds of tongues. The single name of apostleship embraces all these. Let us therefore consult him; let us rather listen to him; let us say to him: Holy Paul the apostle, the monk Pelagius says that you were worthy to receive all the graces of your apostleship; what do you yourself say? I am not worthy, he says, to be called an apostle! Is it so, then, that in order to pay honour to Paul I shall dare to believe Pelagius about Paul rather than Paul?
passages.notes: Reading 'soli' as 'solum'. The final question ('itane, ut deferam...') is construed as ironic.

Nempe etiam inler illa cst, quod objectum cst dixisse Cœlestium , c Dei gratiam secundum inerita nostra dari. > Si crgo veraciter boc Pelagius anathematizavit, quid est quod dicit, gratias omnes Apostolo secundum meritum datas? An aliud est dignumesseaccipera; aliud, secundum meritum accipcre? et potest aliqua subtilitate disputationis ostendere, dignum csse aliqucm, sed uon mereri ?
passages.english: [if he had] looked back at his own most recent reply, and noticed what he anathematized a little before when it was objected to him concerning Caelestius. For indeed among those [statements] is what Caelestius was charged with having said, "that the grace of God is given according to our merits." If then Pelagius truly anathematized this, what does it mean that he says all the graces were given to the Apostle according to merit? Or is it one thing to be worthy to receive, and another to receive according to merit? And can he show by some subtlety of argument that someone is worthy, but does not merit?
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening '[if he had]' is supplied from the conditional in the preceding context.

passages.original: CAPUT XIX. — 45. Ilis rccitatis Synodus dixit: « Quid ad hæc quæ lecta sunt capitula dicit pracseus Pelagius monachus ? Hoc enim reprobat sancta Synodus, et sancta Dei cathoJiea Ecclesia. > Pelagius respondit : « Iterum dico quia hæc et secundum ipsorum testimonium non sunt mea; pro quibus, ut dixi, satisfactionem non debco : quæ vero mea esse confessus sum, hæc recta esse affirmo : qua: autcm dixi non esse mea, secundum judicium sanctae Ecclesiæ reprobo, anathema dicens omni contravenienti et contradicenti sanche catholicæ Ecclesiæ doctrinis.
passages.english: CHAPTER XIX. — 45. When these had been read, the Synod said: "What does the monk Pelagius, who is present, say to these chapters that have been read? For the holy Synod and the holy catholic Church of God reject this." Pelagius replied: "I say again that these things, even according to their own testimony, are not mine; for these, as I said, I owe no satisfaction. But what I have confessed to be mine, I affirm to be correct; and what I have said is not mine, I reject according to the judgement of the holy Church, pronouncing anathema on everyone who goes against and contradicts the teachings of the holy catholic Church.

passages.original: Pervenit in manus noslras nonnulla epistola, quæ ipsius Pelagii diceretur, scribentis ad amicum suum quemdam presbytcrum, qui eum litteris, sicut eadem epistola continetur, benigne admonuerat, ne pcr cjus occasionum se aliquis a corpore Ecclesiæ scpararcl. Ibi inter cætera, quæ inserere longum est, ncc opus cst, ait Pelagius : i Quatuordccim episcoporum sententia definitio nostra com- probata est, qua diximus , posse homiucm sine pcccato csse, et Dci mandata facile custodire, si velit Quæ scnientia, » inquit, t conlradiciionis os1 confusione perfiulil, ct omnem in malum conspiranlem socictatem ab invicem separavit.
passages.english: There came into our hands a certain letter which was said to be Pelagius' own, written to a friend of his, a priest, who, as the same letter states, had kindly warned him by letter that no one should separate himself from the body of the Church on his account. There, among other things which it would take long to set down, and there is no need, Pelagius says: "By the judgement of fourteen bishops our definition has been approved, in which we said that a man can be without sin and easily keep the commandments of God, if he wishes. This judgement," he says, "has covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion, and has split apart from one another the whole fellowship conspiring for evil."
passages.notes: Many scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'noslras' for 'nostras', 'occasionum' for 'occasionem', 'perfiulil' for 'perfudit'). The stray '1' after 'os' is taken as a footnote mark.

passages.original: siasticum judicium ab episcopis quatuordecim factum erat, secandam quod judicium se dixit ista omnia reprobare, et anathema dicere his qui ulia sentiendo, contra judicium veniunt, quod jam tactum fuisse gesta indicant. Jam enim dixerant judices, < Quid ad haec, qune lecta sant capitula, dicit præsens Pelagius monachus? naec enim reprobat sancta Synodus, et sancta Dei catholica Ecclesia. i Sed hoc qui nesciunt, ct istam chartam legunt, putant aliquid illorum licite posse defendi, tamquam non fuerit judicatuin catholicæ contrarium esse doctrinae, paratumque se Pelagius dixerit, id de his rebus sapere, quod Ecclesia non judicavit, sed judicaverit.
passages.english: [...] ecclesiastical judgement had been passed by fourteen bishops, in accordance with which judgement he said that he rejected all these things and pronounced anathema on those who, by thinking otherwise, go against the judgement which the proceedings show had already been given. For the judges had already said: "What does Pelagius the monk, here present, say to these articles which have been read? For the holy Synod and the holy catholic Church of God reject them." But those who do not know this, and read this paper, think that some of those [articles] can lawfully be defended, as if it had not been judged that they were contrary to catholic doctrine, and as if Pelagius had said he was ready to hold, on these matters, what the Church had not [yet] judged but would [at some time] judge.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening words 'jam de his eccl[e]-' are in the context before ('already on these matters [an] ecclesiastical judgement'). 'Tactum' read as 'factum'. The final clause is elliptical; the bracketed '[yet]' and '[at some time]' follow the sense given in the preceding context.
